title: Never to Wonder at Anything
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Meditations by Marcus Aurelius, in the Jeremy Collier translation.
body: From my brother Severus, to be kind and loving to all them of my house and family; by whom also I came to the knowledge of Thrasea and Helvidius, and Cato, and Dio, and Brutus. He it was also that did put me in the first conceit and desire of an equal commonwealth, administered by justice and equality; and of a kingdom wherein should be regarded nothing more than the good and welfare of the subjects. Of him also, to observe a constant tenor, in the study and esteem of philosophy: to be bountiful and liberal in the largest measure; always to hope the best; and to be confident that my friends love me. In whom I moreover observed open dealing towards those whom he reproved at any time, and that his friends might without all doubt or much observation know what he would, or would not, so open and plain was he.

From Claudius Maximus, in all things to endeavour to have power of myself, and in nothing to be carried about; to be cheerful and courageous in all sudden chances and accidents, as in sicknesses: to love mildness, and moderation, and gravity: and to do my business, whatsoever it be, thoroughly, and without querulousness. Whatsoever he said, all men believed him that as he spake, so he thought, and whatsoever he did, that he did it with a good intent. His manner was, never to wonder at anything; never to be in haste, and yet never slow: nor to be perplexed, or dejected, or at any time unseemly, or excessively to laugh: nor to be angry, or suspicious, but ever ready to do good, and to forgive, and to speak truth.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, through whom did the author come to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus?
options: His brother Severus
Claudius Maximus
His father
Alexander the Platonic

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what kind of commonwealth did Severus inspire the author to desire?
options: An equal commonwealth, administered by justice and equality
A commonwealth ruled by a single powerful family
A commonwealth governed entirely by soldiers
A commonwealth without any laws at all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the author learn from Claudius Maximus about facing sudden accidents?
options: To be cheerful and courageous
To seek help from others immediately
To avoid risk whenever possible
To plan carefully in advance for every outcome

questions.prompt: Per the passage, why did all men believe what Claudius Maximus said?
options: Because as he spoke, so he thought
Because he held a position of great political power
Because he always cited other philosophers
Because he repeated himself often

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was Claudius Maximus never, per the author?
options: Perplexed, dejected, or unseemly
Wealthy or well-known
Married or a father
Trained in rhetoric

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say Severus's friends could know his intentions "without all doubt or much observation"?
options: Severus was so open and plain in his dealings that his intentions were never hidden
Severus wrote down all his intentions for others to read
Severus rarely spoke to his friends at all
Severus's intentions were guessed rather than known

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author mention that no one ever felt undervalued by Claudius Maximus?
options: Maximus treated everyone with genuine goodwill rather than condescension
Maximus avoided speaking to most people
Maximus rewarded people financially for their loyalty
Maximus was unaware of how others felt about him

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does it suggest that Claudius Maximus's good conduct seemed entirely his own, natural manner?
options: His good character seemed inborn rather than the result of correcting past faults
He had been trained since childhood by strict tutors
He often pretended to be better than he really was
He copied his behavior directly from Severus

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The author credits Severus and Claudius Maximus with shaping his political ideals and his even, self-possessed character
The author criticizes Severus and Claudius Maximus for their flaws
The author describes a rivalry between Severus and Claudius Maximus
The author explains why he rejected the teachings of both men

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that Claudius Maximus did his business "without querulousness"?
options: Without complaining
Without any assistance
Without proper planning
Without informing others

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the author learn from Severus regarding the study of philosophy?
options: To observe a constant, uninterrupted devotion to it
To study it only in his spare time
To avoid philosophy in favor of politics
To debate philosophers publicly

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the author learn from Severus about his friends?
options: To be confident that his friends love him
To always test his friends' loyalty
To keep his friends at a careful distance
To choose friends only from noble families

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what virtues did the author learn to love from Claudius Maximus?
options: Mildness, moderation, and gravity
Ambition, wealth, and fame
Courage, cunning, and wit
Discipline, silence, and solitude

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what was Claudius Maximus always ready to do?
options: To do good, forgive, and speak truth
To punish wrongdoers severely
To avoid conflict at any cost
To seek advancement in rank

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author emphasize a kingdom that regards "nothing more than the good and welfare of the subjects"?
options: To show that Severus shaped his belief that political power should serve the people rather than the ruler
To argue that all kingdoms are inherently unjust
To explain why Severus opposed all forms of government
To praise a specific king Severus had served

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what the author learned from Claudius Maximus?
options: To remain self-possessed, courageous, and even-tempered no matter what happened
To seek constant praise from others
To avoid taking on any responsibility
To rely on Severus for guidance in all things

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that Claudius Maximus was never "in haste" yet never slow?
options: He acted at a steady, well-timed pace, neither rushed nor sluggish
He refused to make decisions quickly under any circumstance
He was often late to important events
He changed his pace depending on his mood
